ruling_on_a_second_edgar_full_index_vint.question_as_put: Is fetching a SECOND EDGAR full-index vintage worth doing now, given the separation from the 2026-08-16 snapshot would currently be only about 5 weeks?
ruling_on_a_second_edgar_full_index_vint.ruling: CAPTURE YES, ANALYSE NO. Take a dated vintage now and quarterly thereafter as data-foundation hygiene; do NOT attempt first-appearance differencing yet, and do NOT reopen R70_C1 on it.
ruling_on_a_second_edgar_full_index_vint.why_analysis_now_is_worthless: The value of first-appearance differencing scales with the separation relative to the release lag, and R70 measured the release lag directly: UPLOAD rows per quarter collapse monotonically toward the snapshot - 2009q1 3,421; 2015q1 2,494; 2020q1 1,406; 2026q2 351. That right-censoring decays over YEARS. A 5-to-6-week baseline can bound the release instant only for documents that first appear inside those 5-6 weeks, which is a thin and non-random slice - exactly the shortest-lag releases. Imputing a panel-wide release lag from that slice is selection on the dependent variable, and it would produce a confident wrong answer rather than an honest unknown.
ruling_on_a_second_edgar_full_index_vint.why_capture_now_is_still_right: The marginal cost is one HTTP fetch per quarterly index and a few MB. The marginal OPTION value is real and strictly decaying: every month not captured is a month of separation that can never be bought back, and that irreversibility is precisely what made R70_C1 unrecoverable. This is the same discipline as a forward challenger - it converts an unrecoverable historical instant into a prospectively recoverable one - except that it costs no multiple-testing budget and starts no forward clock.
